name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting or directing a trade through more than one on chain liquidity pool rather than accepting the price of a single pool. It sits inside decentralised finance, where automated market makers price assets with a formula and a reserve of tokens instead of an order book. The subject covers the choice of pools, the order in which they are used, and the size of each leg, all aimed at a better net execution than any one venue offers alone. It also covers the aggregators and routers that perform this selection on a user's behalf.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting or directing a trade through more than one on chain liquidity pool rather than accepting the price of a single pool. It sits inside decentralised finance, where automated market makers price assets with a formula and a reserve of tokens instead of an order book. The subject covers the choice of pools, the order in which they are used, and the size of each leg, all aimed at a better net execution than any one venue offers alone. It also covers the aggregators and routers that perform this selection on a user's behalf.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on public blockchains and the smart contracts that hold each pool's reserves. Routers and aggregators read pool state, either directly from the chain or through indexed data services, and simulate candidate paths before submitting a transaction. Execution depends on the block space available, the gas price paid, and the ordering of transactions within a block, which is set by block builders and validators. Because every leg settles on chain, the router must also account for the fees each pool charges and the price impact of its own trade.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A router models each pool's pricing curve, then searches over possible splits and orderings to find the combination with the best output for the requested input. The search is often a graph problem, with pools as edges and tokens as nodes, and it is solved with heuristics or with learned policies when the space is large. Quotes are simulated against current reserves, and the winning route is encoded into a single transaction, sometimes through a dedicated contract that executes the legs atomically. Slippage limits and deadlines are set so the trade reverts if conditions move against it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who controls the route and who bears the loss when it fails. A router is a piece of software, and its operator may take a fee, so users rely on published contracts and audits to judge what it does. Risks include stale quotes, sandwich attacks and other forms of maximal extractable value, failed transactions that still cost gas, and pools whose reserves or admin keys are not what they appear. Provenance matters because the same token can trade under several contracts, and a route through a counterfeit pool can return a worthless asset.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward more of the search happening off chain and more of the settlement happening in batches, which changes who sees a trade before it lands. Intent based systems let a user state an outcome and leave the path to solvers, which shifts the competitive ground from quoting to filling. Cross chain routing extends the same problem across bridges and separate networks, where timing and finality differ. Regulators are paying closer attention to how these venues operate, so the design of routers and the disclosure around them are likely to keep changing.
